text:
Interviewer: This is Jackie Smith interviewing with Mrs. Floor Miller. Today is November 30th, 1994. This is tape one, side one. Mrs. Miller, can you tell me when and where you were born?
Interviewee: I was born January the 1st, 1925, in Brzeziny, Poland.
Interviewer: Could you tell me where Brzeziny is?
Interviewee: Brzeziny is a little town near Lodz.
Interviewer: Could you tell me something about your family? How large was your family? What did your dad do?
Interviewee: My, the family was my father, mother, a sister, two brothers, then it’s me and another sister. We were five siblings.
Interviewer: Could you tell me what your father did for a living?
Interviewee: We had a, we were shoe manufacturers. We had a store, and we manufactured our own shoes.
Interviewer: Was it a religious house?
Interviewee: Yes, it was. Not strictly, but religious.
Interviewer: Could you tell me a little bit about your life before the war?
Interviewee: Just like a typical youngster. I just finished seventh grade of public school, which I believe it’s like here high school. And I went to Bet Jacob. I went after school. I went to Bet Jacob.
Interviewer: Bet Jacob was a religious...
Interviewee: A religious school, yes. And just like a typical teenager, dancing and singing and living it well, which I understood, except the antisemitism was strong, which I understood already that this country is not good for Jews.
Interviewer: In what way did you experience antisemitism?
Interviewee: One morning, we wake up and in our front door of the store was all kind of signs, “Don’t Buy By The Jews, The Jews Are Your Enemies.” And on top of our name from the store it was somebody’s sign of a store that sold tref, pig...
Interviewer: Pigs?
Interviewee: Pigs, and kielbasi and so. It was, they put on on our front door.
Interviewer: The door. I assume that your house was a kosher house?
Interviewee: Yes, yes.
Interviewer: Your mother kept kosher.
Interviewee: Yes.
Interviewer: Do you remember if your father went to synagogue regularly?
Interviewee: Yes, every Saturday. And in the morning he put on tefillin, and the tallit, and so did my brothers.
Interviewer: O.K. Did you belong to any Zionist organization or did any of your brothers or sisters belong to Zionist organizations?
Interviewee: I remember my brother, Moniek, he belonged to a Zionist organization. I wasn’t allowed because I was too young. They were very strict. My parents were very strict with us. But my father was a Zionist. He was in Israel till 19-, like ’20 he came back. He was there a long time. In fact he was fighting with Trumpeldor.
Interviewer: Trumpeldor.
Interviewee: Trumpeldor, yes. He was in the Legion and also got injured.
Interviewer: Oh, he was injured. Did any of your family serve in the Polish Army?
Interviewee: Yes, my brother Moniek.
Interviewer: Do you remember when he was called to the army?
Interviewee: No. I just remember he came back in a uniform, and he looked so gorgeous, so handsome.
Interviewer: Do you know how many Jews lived in Brzeziny? Approximately, was...
Interviewee: Fifteen for sure, fifteen thousand for sure.
Interviewer: And that would be what percentage of the whole population? Would you say it’s ten percent?
Interviewee: That’s from the city?
Interviewer: Yeah.
Interviewee: No, it was more than ten percent. It must be thirty-five percent.
Interviewer: O.K., about thirty-five percent. Were most Jews there Orthodox?
Interviewee: No.
Interviewer: No. Now, could you tell me what happened when the war broke out? How did it affect you, the first days of the war, in September of 1939?
Interviewee: We were still in the country. We were still...
Interviewer: You were on vacation?
Interviewee: On...
Interviewer: You say in the country.
Interviewee: We had my mother always rented, my parents always rented a room in the woods. It was called Siemieniczki.
Interviewer: Siemieniczki.
Interviewee: Niczki, yeah. This was like five miles behind the city. It was the woods. And we, for the summer we had there a room and we stayed there short before the holidays and we came back for the holidays. But that summer I remember it was the 30th of August. My mother came and to pick us up much earlier than we were supposed to come, and she says, “It’s terrible things happening in the world and I want you all home, children.” And I was looking at my mother’s gray face, and I asked, “Why? What happened? What happened?” She told me that the war is going on. I said, “War? What can be so bad, the war?” But little did I know.
Interviewer: So you came back to Brzeziny. Do you remember when the Germans marched in and what happened?
Interviewee: They marched in on September, ‘39, came out the war. They must have marched in the second or the third day.
Interviewer: Did they immediately start persecution of the Jews?
Interviewee: Yes. First they bombed the city, which was a lot of casualties.
Interviewer: Right.
Interviewee: I remember a young boy, a little young boy they had, a bullet hit him in the head and a ear got teared off.
Interviewer: Got torn off.
Interviewee: This was the first shtick that I saw. And I was running out from the house, and I saw the bullets knocking against the stones in the yard. But I was running towards my father, because they were in a bigger building and we owned. And then right away they occupied. And if not they didn’t do the job, the Polaks, the Polish people do the job. They, right away they robbed us.
Interviewer: The Poles did?
Interviewee: The Poles, yes. They robbed us.
Interviewer: Now, tell me, were you allowed still to go to school after the Germans marched in?
Interviewee: No.
Interviewer: No. Were you confined into a ghetto?
Interviewee: Yes.
Interviewer: And that was almost immediately? Or do you remember when?
Interviewee: No. It wasn’t right away. It was maybe a few weeks or, I rather not say it for sure because I don’t remember. But it was very quick done that we were, we had to stay in one place.
Interviewer: Was your father allowed to continue to work in his store?
Interviewee: But we were robbed, so it was nothing to work anymore.
Interviewer: Oh, you made...
Interviewee: A little bit that we was, we were hiding some shoes that my father said, “My children will need some shoes.” So this is what it was.
Interviewer: Then the...
Interviewee: So we right away find out what hunger is too.
Interviewer: So you were robbed right in the beginning of that.
Interviewee: Right in the beginning, by the Polish people, from our Polish neighbors.
Interviewer: Now, were you obligated to wear an arm band, or a yellow star?
Interviewee: Yes, a yellow star, from both sides, on the front and in the back.
Interviewer: The back, on the shoul-, near the shoulder. Could you tell me, when they started to organize the ghetto, was this in a specific part of the city that they, everybody had to move into?
Interviewee: Not so much in Brzeziny, not so much. Well, we remained at the same address. We remained. But I don’t remember too much from Brzeziny, because I remained in the same place.
Interviewer: You remained in this...
Interviewee: Yes.
Interviewer: Was...
Interviewee: But we were, we got a Sperre. We’re not allowed to go out in the evening, so, when that twilight came.
Interviewer: Was the ghetto surrounded by a wall or by wires, or by...
Interviewee: Wires.
